source.title: It’s a (Blind) Match! Towards Vision-Language Correspondence without Parallel Data
source.authors: Dominik Schnaus; Nikita Araslanov; Daniel Cremers

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present; no apparent truncation or garbling affects the extracted results.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures vision-language alignment across model capacities and reports no clear improvement with larger models; it also shows that alignment depends on the metric and selected classes.
record.gate_note: Included matching-accuracy, geometry-metric, capacity-sweep, class-subset, and shuffling results. The classifier results are not included because classification accuracy is not itself a representation-alignment measure. Solver comparisons are omitted because their differences primarily measure solver performance.
record.test_reason: The study measures how well class-level embeddings from 32 vision and 27 language models align, using matching accuracy and Mutual k-NN. Its capacity sweeps within five vision families show no clear gain in alignment with size, against the scaling part of V1 and V2. It also shows alignment depends on which classes are chosen and is far from complete at larger problem sizes.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that blind vision-language matching is feasible for many small problems and for some larger, well-chosen subsets, but not for arbitrary categories with current models. Pretraining method shapes alignment more than model size, and larger vision models do not necessarily align better on CIFAR-10 or CINIC-10. They speculate scaling may still help on other data such as WIT. Language supervision (CLIP) seems to help with fine-grained classes.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures within-modality pairwise geometry and solves a quadratic assignment problem to infer cross-modal class correspondences without parallel data; it is not a direct reproduction of the original scale-alignment measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Matching outcomes vary with metric (Mutual k-NN, CKA, or Gromov-Wasserstein), dataset, selected class subsets, problem size, and pretraining strategy. The capacity sweeps show no clear size trend.

fits_no_version.finding: Randomly initialised ViT-H/14 models and raw pixel values show the same monotone drop in alignment under shuffling as pretrained encoders, though at lower absolute values. The authors attribute this to pixel statistics and to networks roughly preserving distances (Lipschitz constant near 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-modal alignment metrics register some structure even for untrained encoders or raw pixels, so part of the measured alignment may reflect low-level image statistics.

record.peer_reviewed: To appear in Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 2025
record.problems: Capacity trends are tested with language models held fixed, and model capability is not independently measured. The larger-problem results use deliberately optimized class subsets rather than arbitrary classes. Several relevant trends are presented only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted solver-comparison rows and unsupervised-classifier accuracies: these report solver or downstream classification performance rather than an additional alignment result. Supplementary Tables 1, 6, and 7 and main-text Table 2.

untested.parts: Only vision-model size is varied, with the language model fixed. Capability is not measured independently. Convergence across arbitrary architectures within one modality is not tested.
Language-model scale is not swept, and the two models are never improved together. Alignment is not related to measured performance.
Entirely untested: no seed or initialisation comparisons.
No dense or linear maps, stitching, or reconstruction loss are tested. Only class-level correspondence recovery is measured.
Entirely untested: no features or circuits are examined.
The number of neighbours k (fixed at 5) is not varied, and out-of-distribution inputs are not tested.
There is no causal separation of shared data or objectives from a common model of reality, and no test for a plateau.

missing.what: Shuffling curves for random ViTs and raw pixel values, compared with pretrained models
Matching accuracy for every vision × language model combination (27 language models). DINOv2 averages 5.3% (CIFAR-10) and 7.6% (CINIC-10) above the next-best pretraining strategy.

Dataset dependence: the same classes match differently on CIFAR-10 and on CINIC-10 (ImageNet resolution), e.g. CLIP with all-mpnet 20.5% vs 50%. The authors also say scaling may help on WIT but not on every dataset.
Unsupervised classifier accuracy (28.6–51.1% against a 10% baseline), i.e. correspondence without paired data applied to clusters

record.verdict_notes: I reclassified the shuffling rows (r23–r27) as not bearing on V6: they validate the metrics rather than show convergence depends on them. I added V4, since the paper's core result is recovering correspondence without paired data. r7 probably names the wrong language model. The metric-comparison rows (r1–r6) compare the study's own objective choices and the differences are modest. The original sources (the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and Convergent Learning) are not this study, so verdicts are allowed.

versions.untested_parts: The scale sweep varies vision-model size while holding the language model fixed; it does not test scaling both modalities or model capability directly. It also does not test convergence across arbitrary architectures, objectives, and data at scale.

The study measures image-text correspondence and varies vision-model capacity with language models fixed. It does not test simultaneous improvements in both modalities or relate alignment to independently measured performance.
Different initializations of the same architecture and shared features or subspaces across seeds are not tested.
The study finds category correspondences from pairwise geometry; it does not test representation transfer, stitching, or loss under a map between embedding spaces.
Recurring interpretable features or circuits are not examined.
The paper varies metrics and inputs/classes, but does not systematically test neighborhood-count settings or out-of-distribution inputs.

The paper reports incomplete and class-dependent matching and discusses pretraining effects, but does not causally separate shared training data/objectives from a common model of reality, nor establish a scaling plateau.

labels.reason: Appendix F.1 explicitly reports no clear increase in matching accuracy or Mutual k-NN with vision capacity for these datasets (r9–r16).

labels.label: challenges
labels.condition: The same vision-capacity sweeps against All-Roberta-large-v1 and all-mpnet-base-v2
labels.reason: The vision-size implication fails in this class-level setting (r9–r16). Language-model improvement and joint capability scaling remain untested.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Existence of above-chance image–text class alignment at N=10 (CIFAR-10 and CINIC-10)
labels.reason: Above-chance correspondence at fixed model pairs establishes alignment, but does not test V2's increase with model improvement (r1–r8).

labels.label: limits_scope

labels.reason: These experiments vary class subsets and problem size while fixing checkpoints; they do not test V2's model-improvement trend (r17–r22).

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Class-level correspondence recovered without paired data
labels.reason: Class correspondences are recoverable without parallel data, but recovery becomes incomplete for larger selected problems (r7,r8,r17–r22). The 80% CIFAR-10 result uses MPNet.

labels.reason: Table 3 retains substantial matching across objectives: 59–69.5% on CIFAR-10 and 70–80% on CINIC-10 (r1–r6). This is descriptive robustness, without a significance test of metric differences.

labels.reason: Section 4.2 explicitly reports category dependence; Section 5.2 shows declining correspondence as selected problems grow (r17–r22).

relation.reason: The study measures cross-modal geometry, matching accuracy and capacity trends, beyond using alignment for its proposed application.

tranche.reason: Its capacity sweeps explicitly question general alignment gains with model size, and its larger problems show incomplete correspondence.

source_check.notes: Larger-problem results use selected favorable subsets; imperfect optimization also limits interpretation because global optimality is generally unavailable at large N. Class matching does not establish dense representation interchangeability or convergence with jointly improving model capability.
